messages.author: 93fdeb4704061276
messages.subject: g++ profiling on sampling function?
parts:
I'm doing tech support on one of the student projects. I'm looking for a command line/Unix user who can point me in the right direction. I want to know how to profile Stan's internal activities, the C++ side calculations.

A user here wants to run 1000s of variants of an MCMC rstan project. On the compute cluster, for some not-yet-solved-reason, the completion of a chain with 10000 iterations requires 24 hours (but it takes 12 hours on my RedHat Linux workstations).  We have ruled out the usual sources of slowdown, such as disk writes or memory swapping.  The R profile seems to indicate that almost all of the time is spent in the Rstan "sampling" function. I started to wonder what I can do to quantify the limitations on the program. 

Can I find somebody who runs the command line Stan who can tell me if it is possible to run g++ in profiling mode?

I've been reading the Stan programming manual and I gather there is a way to compile a stan project to run from the command line.  As in all programming manuals, I  understand that there are many "dos and don'ts" for writing a fast model.  Without becoming a Stan expert, recognizing certain "bad tendencies" in user code, its not clear what I ought to do.   I'd really like to have a profile. Over the years, I've had plenty of examples where the profiler points at slow spots that you would never guess.

I've not done this in a while, but I'm pretty sure I'd need to rebuild Stan itself with profiling and debugging symbols. After that, I have some experience in other C and Objective-C projects, but not in C++.

Paul Johnson

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: g++ profiling on sampling function?
parts:
On Friday, May 5, 2017 at 12:21:04 AM UTC-4, Paul Johnson wrote:
Can I find somebody who runs the command line Stan who can tell me if it is possible to run g++ in profiling mode?

One can download or git clone CmdStan from

https://github.com/stan-dev/cmdstan/

and execute

make stan-update
make -j8 build
echo "CFLAGS += -pg" >> make/local
make /path/to/stanfile/without/dotstan/extension

Followed by

cd /path/to/directory/with/stanfile
./executable_name sample data file = my.data.R

where the my.data.R file has to be created from R using rstan::rstan::stan_rdump() . And then do the usual gprof stuff.

However, when you do all that, you will find that almost all of the time is spent evaluating the gradient, which is not that useful unless you are prepared to write C++ functions that substitute analytical gradient calculations for Stan's autodiff. Maybe it comes to that, but usually the place to start is with the model and the geometry of the posterior distribution it implies. By default Stan does up to 2^10 - 1 gradient evaluations per MCMC iteration, but will do fewer if it hits the U-turn point on each MCMC iteration before doing 10 leapfrog steps. So, if you can go from 9 leapfrog steps to 6 with various reparameterizations, then it will take much less time to run.

Ben

We have ruled out the usual sources of slowdown, such as disk writes or memory swapping. The R profile seems to indicate that almost all of the time is spent in the Rstan "sampling" function. I started to wonder what I can do to quantify the limitations on the program.
Your best bet is to have the student send us the program so we can help optimize it.

> Can I find somebody who runs the command line Stan who can tell me if it is possible to run g++ in profiling mode?
>
> I've been reading the Stan programming manual and I gather there is a way to compile a stan project to run from the command line. As in all programming manuals, I understand that there are many "dos and don'ts" for writing a fast model. Without becoming a Stan expert, recognizing certain "bad tendencies" in user code, its not clear what I ought to do. I'd really like to have a profile. Over the years, I've had plenty of examples where the profiler points at slow spots that you would never guess.

So have we all. We're always happy to take performance improvement pull requests if you can find a problem.

I should warn you up front that our code is very tightly dependent on our low-level memory allocation and inlining at optimization level -O3. Profiling at -O0, etc. won't help, and when you run at -O3 so much is inlined that it's hard to see down into the lower-level code. You can also run into bias issues where simple instrumentation of the code provides very different answers than profiling.

Any help here would be appreciated, too.

> I've not done this in a while, but I'm pretty sure I'd need to rebuild Stan itself with profiling and debugging symbols. After that, I have some experience in other C and Objective-C projects, but not in C++.

You may find the C++ a bit daunting in Stan---it's heavily templated with a ton of metaprogramming. But as Ben says, what we see under profiling is that almost all the time's spent in computing the backward pass of automatic differentiation for gradients. It's effectively interpreted code for computing the chain rule.

- Bob

The usual suspects for cluster slowdown are:

* high latency file I/O

* limited memory

* memory/CPU contention from shared jobs

We haven't paid a lot of attention to any of these issues,
I'm afraid, so any improvements to the base code for these
situations would be appreciated.

If you send us your Stan code, we can help optimize.

This list is shutting down, so if you wouldn't mind, please
take this up again here in a new thread:

http://discourse.mc-stan.org

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] g++ profiling on sampling function?
parts:
On Tuesday, May 9, 2017 at 9:52:09 AM UTC-4, jbru...@gmail.com wrote:
Most perplexing to me is the difference in run time across systems. It takes Paul 12 hours on his RedHat workstations, and I've clocked it at 10-12 hours on my Windows workstation. The fact that it takes twice as long to run on the cluster is baffling!

I would guess that the cluster nodes are not picking up the CXXFLAGS in your ~/.R/Makevars file. If you call stan_model() with verbose = TRUE, you can see the compiler output in the logs to see what optimization level it used.

Ben
